misconception_pool.misconception: Deleting an uploaded photo or post immediately removes it from internet storage systems.
misconception_pool.fact: Erased online content often remains cached on external indexing servers and private archives.

misconception_pool.misconception: Deleting a social media post from your profile immediately erases every copy of that content from the internet.
misconception_pool.fact: Other users can screenshot posts within seconds, and third-party web archives or server backups often retain copies indefinitely.

misconception_pool.misconception: Setting a social media account to private prevents mobile apps from collecting your device location and contact list.
misconception_pool.fact: Account visibility only restricts other users; you must revoke OS-level location and contact permissions to stop app data collection.

misconception_pool.misconception: Incognito or private browsing mode hides your internet activity from your internet service provider and school network.
misconception_pool.fact: Private browsing only prevents your local browser from saving history and cookies; networks and websites still see your traffic.

misconception_pool.misconception: Strangers in online gaming lobbies only know the profile information you explicitly type into the text chat window.
misconception_pool.fact: Voice chat background noise, reused usernames, and linked platform accounts can reveal your real identity and physical location.

requirements.req_text: Cyber Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Attacks. Do the following and discuss each with your counselor: (a) Define the terms vulnerability, threat, and exploit, and give an example of each that might apply to a website or software product you use. (b) Pick one type of malware (such as virus, worm, Trojan, backdoor, spyware, or ransomware) and find out how it works. Explain what it does and the harm it can cause. (c) Identify two risks of using public Wi-Fi and describe how to reduce or avoid those risks. (d) Describe what spoofing and phishing are, and how to recognize a message or website that might be trying to trick you. Explain what steps you should take to protect yourself and others if you come across one. (e) Current Events. Do ONE of the following: (1) Read an article or a news report about a recent cybersecurity incident, such as a data breach or malware infection. Explain how the incident happened (to the best of your ability based on the information available) and what the consequences are or might be to the victim. (2) With your parent or guardian's permission, watch a movie or read a book in which cybersecurity plays a significant role. Discuss how cybersecurity topics were depicted and how realistic you think it was. (f) Create a list of what is part of your cyber attack surface including all the ways someone could try to access your personal information or devices, such as online accounts, apps, or home networks.

misconception_pool.misconception: The terms threat, vulnerability, and exploit describe the exact same security concept.
misconception_pool.fact: Attacks succeed when a specific threat actively leverages an unpatched software flaw.

misconception_pool.misconception: A software vulnerability and an exploit are two interchangeable words for the same piece of malicious computer code.
misconception_pool.fact: A vulnerability is a weakness in software or hardware, whereas an exploit is the specific tool or technique used to trigger that weakness.

misconception_pool.misconception: Computer worms require a human user to open an infected email attachment or click a malicious file before they can spread.
misconception_pool.fact: Worms self-replicate automatically across networks by exploiting unpatched network service vulnerabilities without any user interaction.

misconception_pool.misconception: Trojan horse malware replicates itself into other system files on your hard drive just like a traditional file-infecting virus.
misconception_pool.fact: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick the user into running it, rather than self-replicating into other files.

misconception_pool.misconception: Paying the demanded cryptocurrency ransom after a ransomware attack guarantees that criminals will restore all of your files.
misconception_pool.fact: Attackers frequently fail to provide working decryption keys, retain stolen data for extortion, and target paying victims again.

requirements.req_text: Cyber Defenses. Do the following: (a) Describe three technologies that are used to defend a computer or network, such as access controls, antivirus software, firewall, intrusion detection/prevention systems, and Virtual Private Network. (b) Installing updates. Do the following: (1) Explain to your counselor the importance of installing the latest updates on your computer, why they are needed, and what kinds of problems they can prevent. (2) Demonstrate to your counselor how to check for, download, and install the latest updates for your computer or mobile device, or another computer you have permission to use. (If you are unable to do this on your computer, you may use an online guide with screenshots to demonstrate this.) Show your counselor how to verify that your computer or mobile device is up-to-date. (c) System security. With your parent or guardian's permission, do THREE of the following using a computer or mobile device, and discuss with your counselor: (1) Describe what makes a good password and why. Set or change an account password to one that is "strong." (2) Describe multi-factor authentication (MFA) and how it can be used to improve security. Demonstrate how to use an authenticator app or other MFA function. (3) Install and set up a password manager. Demonstrate how it works to your counselor. (4) Run a virus scan. Show the results to your counselor. (5) Using a command line or other built-in tool, see what programs or processes are running on your computer. Discuss with your counselor what you see and what surprises you. (6) Use a command line interface to view your computer's open network connections. Discuss the results with your counselor. (7) Demonstrate how to back up your data from a mobile device to a local computer or the cloud. (8) Research best practices for protecting a home computer or network, and make a checklist of FIVE things you and your family can do to stay secure. (9) Identify one or more other vulnerabilities on your home computer or network or another computer or network you have permission to use and discuss with your counselor. With permission from the system owner, take the necessary actions to fix it.

requirements.description: Cyber Defenses. Do the following: (a) Describe three technologies that are used to defend a computer or network, such as access controls, antivirus software, firewall, intrusion detection/prevention systems, and Virtual Private Network. (b) Installing updates. Do the following: (1) Explain to your counselor the importance of installing the latest updates on your computer, why they are needed, and what kinds of problems they can prevent. (c) System security. With your parent or guardian's permission, do THREE of the following using a computer or mobile device, and discuss with your counselor: (1) Describe what makes a good password and why. Set or change an account password to one that is "strong." (2) Describe multi-factor authentication (MFA) and how it can be used to improve security. Demonstrate how to use an authenticator app or other MFA function. (3) Install and set up a password manager. Demonstrate how it works to your counselor. (4) Run a virus scan. Show the results to your counselor. (5) Using a command line or other built-in tool, see what programs or processes are running on your computer. Discuss with your counselor what you see and what surprises you. (6) Use a command line interface to view your computer's open network connections. Discuss the results with your counselor. (7) Demonstrate how to back up your data from a mobile device to a local computer or the cloud. (8) Research best practices for protecting a home computer or network, and make a checklist of FIVE things you and your family can do to stay secure. (9) Identify one or more other vulnerabilities on your home computer or network or another computer or network you have permission to use and discuss with your counselor. misconception_pool.misconception: Software updates exist solely to introduce visual interface changes and new software features.
misconception_pool.fact: Software patches address discovered security vulnerabilities alongside general functional bug repairs.

misconception_pool.misconception: Connecting through a Virtual Private Network makes your computer immune to phishing websites and downloaded malware payloads.
misconception_pool.fact: A VPN only encrypts traffic in transit between your device and the VPN server; it does not block malicious downloads or fake login pages.

misconception_pool.misconception: Enabling a network firewall removes the need to install regular security patches on your operating system and web browser.
misconception_pool.fact: Firewalls allow normal web and email traffic on permitted ports, so unpatched browsers and apps remain vulnerable to exploits.

misconception_pool.misconception: Signature-based antivirus software automatically detects and blocks every brand-new zero-day malware strain on arrival.
misconception_pool.fact: Traditional signature scanners only recognize known malware hashes and must pair with behavioral heuristics to catch novel threats.

requirements.req_text: Cryptography. Do the following: (a) Research and explain to your counselor three situations where encryption is used in cybersecurity. For each situation, describe what kind of encryption is used and why it is important. (b) Show how you can know if your connection to a website is encrypted. (c) Do ONE of the following: (1) Create your own encryption code, such as a substitution cipher or code book, and demonstrate using it to encrypt and decrypt a message. requirements.description: Cryptography. Do the following: (a) Research and explain to your counselor three situations where encryption is used in cybersecurity. For each situation, describe what kind of encryption is used and why it is important. (b) Show how you can know if your connection to a website is encrypted. (c) Do ONE of the following: (1) Create your own encryption code, such as a substitution cipher or code book, and demonstrate using it to encrypt and decrypt a message. Describe the strengths and weaknesses of your code. (2) Download and set up an app (from an official app store) that uses end-to-end encryption. Explain to your counselor what this means, how it works, and why it is more secure than other forms of communication (e. g. SMS). (3) Use a hashing tool (for example, using SHA or MD5) to create a checksum for a file, document, or piece of text. Have a fellow Scout or your counselor make a change to it, then recreate the checksum and compare the new checksum to the original as a demonstration of file integrity checking. (4) Create your own PGP (pretty good privacy) email key. Share your public key with others (and your counselor). Also, get their public keys and add them to your computer's key ring. Send a message that has been digitally encrypted.

misconception_pool.misconception: Encryption makes data completely unreadable only to attackers while keeping it readable to intermediaries.
misconception_pool.fact: Modern transport layer security encrypts web traffic using asymmetric key exchange and symmetric ciphers.

misconception_pool.misconception: The padlock icon and HTTPS prefix in a browser address bar prove that the website owner is trustworthy and safe from fraud.
misconception_pool.fact: HTTPS only proves that traffic between your browser and that server is encrypted; phishing sites routinely obtain valid TLS certificates.

misconception_pool.misconception: Asymmetric public-key encryption is used to encrypt every megabyte of video and file traffic during an HTTPS web session.
misconception_pool.fact: Asymmetric cryptography is slow and is only used during the TLS handshake to exchange a fast symmetric key like AES for bulk data.

misconception_pool.misconception: In public-key cryptography, you must keep both your public key and your private key secret from everyone on the network.
misconception_pool.fact: Your public key is shared openly so others can encrypt messages or verify signatures, while only your private key remains secret.

misconception_pool.misconception: Full-disk encryption on a laptop protects your files from remote hackers while you are logged in and browsing the internet.
misconception_pool.fact: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest when the device is powered off or locked, not while the operating system has mounted the drive.

What physical safety risks arise if an attacker compromises a connected home thermostat?
How does segmenting home networks into guest virtual local area networks protect smart devices?
What router configuration step isolates smart cameras and thermostats from the laptops that store your family tax records?
Which hardware and software limitations make smart home sensors harder to patch and monitor than a standard desktop computer?

misconception_pool.misconception: Home internet appliances lack sufficient computational power to participate in malicious botnet swarms.
misconception_pool.fact: Default manufacturer credentials on smart devices are indexed in publicly accessible online registries.

misconception_pool.misconception: Smart lightbulbs and Wi-Fi thermostats have no personal files on them, so hackers have no reason to target those devices.
misconception_pool.fact: Attackers compromise poorly secured IoT devices to assemble massive botnets like Mirai or to pivot into laptops on the same local network.

misconception_pool.misconception: Setting a strong Wi-Fi network password protects smart cameras even if you leave their factory admin password unchanged.
misconception_pool.fact: Cloud vulnerabilities, Universal Plug and Play port forwarding, or local malware can still access devices using default credentials.

misconception_pool.misconception: Internet of Things devices automatically receive lifetime security updates from their manufacturer without user intervention.
misconception_pool.fact: Many low-cost IoT vendors stop releasing firmware patches after a few years, leaving older devices permanently exposed to exploits.

misconception_pool.misconception: Connecting smart home gadgets and work computers to the same single Wi-Fi subnet provides the safest home network layout.
misconception_pool.fact: Placing IoT devices on a separate guest VLAN prevents a compromised smart appliance from scanning or attacking your personal computers.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Cybersecurity Requirement 1, how do the three pillars of the CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability) protect an organization's information systems?
options: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls).
B. Confidentiality means keeping software bugs secret from programmers, Integrity means never updating operating systems.
C. The CIA Triad requires sharing a single administrator password across all staff members so nobody is ever locked out of the network.
D. Confidentiality deletes all files after twenty-four hours, Integrity blocks antivirus scanners.
choices: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls).
B. Confidentiality means keeping software bugs secret from programmers, Integrity means never updating operating systems.
C. The CIA Triad requires sharing a single administrator password across all staff members so nobody is ever locked out of the network.
D. Confidentiality deletes all files after twenty-four hours, Integrity blocks antivirus scanners.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data (via encryption and access controls), Integrity ensures data is not secretly altered or tampered with (via cryptographic hashes), and Availability ensures authorized users can reliably access systems when needed (via backups and DDoS mitigation).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The CIA Triad is the core model of information security: Confidentiality protects privacy, Integrity guards accuracy and trustworthiness against tampering, and Availability keeps systems operational for legitimate users.

choices: A. Public Wi-Fi signals drain laptop batteries faster and corrupt local hard drive sectors
